title: We Built It Here in Ghana

pages.text: During the bumper harvest season near Sunyani, fourteen-year-old Mansa and her cousin Mensah stood beside Auntie Yaa’s farm truck in frustration. Heaps of golden ripe plantains and fresh cassava tubers lay unsold at the roadside because every farmer had harvested at the exact same week! Meanwhile, inside town supermarkets, shoppers paid high prices for imported biscuits and crisps shipped from thousands of kilometres away.
sentences: During the bumper harvest season near Sunyani, fourteen-year-old Mansa and her cousin Mensah stood beside Auntie Yaa’s farm truck in frustration.
Heaps of golden ripe plantains and fresh cassava tubers lay unsold at the roadside because every farmer had harvested at the exact same week!
Meanwhile, inside town supermarkets, shoppers paid high prices for imported biscuits and crisps shipped from thousands of kilometres away.
pages.alt: Fourteen-year-old Mansa and Mensah stand with Auntie Yaa beside unsold heaps of ripe plantains while a supermarket across the road displays imported snacks.

pages.text: ‘Why do raw plantains and cassava spoil so fast after harvest?’ Mansa asked in her JHS Career Technology class. Her teacher explained that fresh tubers and ripe plantains contain high moisture, which allows moulds and enzymes to break them down within days. ‘Agro-processing,’ the teacher said, ‘uses food science — drying, slicing, roasting or milling — to remove moisture, extend shelf life for months, and add value right here in Ghana!’

‘Agro-processing,’ the teacher said, ‘uses food science — drying, slicing, roasting or milling — to remove moisture, extend shelf life for months, and add value right here in Ghana!’
pages.alt: In the JHS Career Technology room, Mansa and Mensah compare fresh high-moisture plantains with shelf-stable dried plantain crisps and cassava flour.

pages.text: That school project planted a lifelong dream. Years later, after Mansa studied food science and Mensah studied accounting, the two cousins pooled their savings with four local farmers to start a small agro-processing workshop. Their goal was simple: turn Auntie Yaa’s surplus plantains and cassava into lightly salted baked plantain crisps and high-quality composite baking flour.
sentences: That school project planted a lifelong dream.
Years later, after Mansa studied food science and Mensah studied accounting, the two cousins pooled their savings with four local farmers to start a small agro-processing workshop.
Their goal was simple: turn Auntie Yaa’s surplus plantains and cassava into lightly salted baked plantain crisps and high-quality composite baking flour.
pages.alt: Now young adults in their twenties, Mansa and Mensah set up a small clean food-processing room with stainless-steel tables.

pages.text: Building a real manufacturing business in Ghana was not easy! In their second month, they applied for a commercial bank loan to buy a bigger dehydrator, but the bank’s interest rate was twenty-eight percent a year — far too high for a young workshop with small sales. Instead of taking a reckless loan that could crush them, Mensah negotiated a phased equipment lease with an agricultural development fund and reinvested every cedi of early profit.
sentences: Building a real manufacturing business in Ghana was not easy!

pages.alt: Mensah and Mansa review loan interest calculations at a desk and choose an affordable phased equipment lease instead.

pages.text: Next came an engineering setback. Their first locally fabricated hot-air dryer heated unevenly: trays at the bottom scorched dark brown, while trays at the top stayed damp and chewy! Twenty batches were ruined. Mansa did not hide the mistake or sell burnt crisps. Working with a local metal fabricator, she installed a baffle plate and a thermostat fan that circulated warm air evenly across all twelve trays.

Working with a local metal fabricator, she installed a baffle plate and a thermostat fan that circulated warm air evenly across all twelve trays.
pages.alt: Mansa and a local technician install an air-circulation fan and thermostat inside the stainless-steel drying cabinet.

pages.text: Before they could sell to supermarkets, schools and hospitals, they had to meet strict national law. Mr Ofori from the Food and Drugs Authority — FDA Ghana — inspected their premises alongside standards guidelines from the Ghana Standards Authority — GSA. He checked handwashing stations, hairnets, pest screens, batch expiry dates, and tested the flour’s moisture content to ensure it was below twelve percent so mould could never grow.

pages.alt: FDA inspector Mr Ofori checks the stainless-steel hygiene stations and tests flour moisture while Mansa and Mensah take notes.

pages.text: When a distributor tempted Mensah to skip the final laboratory test and print a fake registration number to get onto shelves two months early, Mensah refused flatly. ‘If one child gets sick from unverified food, our reputation and our conscience are ruined forever,’ he said. Three months later, after passing every lab test honestly, their packs proudly carried a genuine FDA registration number!

pages.alt: Mensah firmly rejects a shortcut while Mansa holds up their official FDA food-safety certificate and sealed crisp pouches.

pages.text: Mensah tracked the unit economics of every hundred-pack batch with precision. Buying fresh plantains directly from Auntie Yaa’s cooperative cost two hundred cedis. Washing, slicing, baking, solar-assisted drying, moisture-proof pouches and FDA-compliant labels cost one hundred and fifty cedis — making a total production cost of three hundred and fifty cedis for one hundred packs, or three cedis fifty pesewas per pack.
sentences: Mensah tracked the unit economics of every hundred-pack batch with precision.
Buying fresh plantains directly from Auntie Yaa’s cooperative cost two hundred cedis.

pages.alt: Mensah writes the batch cost breakdown on a whiteboard: 200 cedis raw plantains + 150 cedis processing and packaging = 350 cedis for 100 packs.

pages.text: They priced each pack wholesale at five cedis. Selling one hundred packs brought in five hundred cedis of revenue! Subtracting the three-hundred-and-fifty-cedi total cost left one hundred and fifty cedis of gross profit per batch — a healthy thirty percent margin that paid workers’ wages, factory rent, electricity and savings for a second production line.

pages.alt: Mansa and Mensah stack 100 sealed packs into shipping cartons, earning 500 cedis in revenue and 150 cedis in gross profit.

pages.text: Even with a great product, market competition was fierce. At first, two big city supermarkets placed their Ghanaian packs on the bottom shelf behind imported brands. Mansa and Mensah responded with smart marketing: they offered free taste tests outside schools and offices, designed bright moisture-lock pouches that kept crisps crunchy for six months, and delivered on time every single Monday.

pages.alt: At a clean supermarket tasting counter, shoppers happily sample the crunchy Ghanaian plantain crisps and pick up packs from a top display.

pages.text: After four years of steady work, the impact reached across the district. The factory employed eighteen full-time workers — food technicians, machine operators, quality clerks and drivers — all enrolled in SSNIT pensions, and signed guaranteed purchase contracts with forty-five smallholder farmers led by Auntie Yaa. Post-harvest plantain losses in their cooperative dropped by more than half!

pages.alt: Outside the expanded solar-roofed agro-processing facility, Mansa, Mensah and Auntie Yaa stand proudly with the 18 factory staff and visiting farmers.

pages.text: When JHS students from Sunyani toured the plant on Career Day, Mansa handed each student a warm, crunchy sample pack. ‘We did not build this overnight, and nobody handed us easy millions,’ she told them with a proud smile. ‘We combined science, honest accounting, food-safety law and persistence. Ghana grows the finest harvests on Earth — and your generation can process, package and share them with the world!’

activities.question: How does agro-processing stop fresh cassava and ripe plantains from spoiling within a few days?
options: By removing moisture and sealing hygienically to extend shelf life and add value
By leaving raw heaps of fruit in the hot roadside sun
By painting raw plantains with blue ink
activities.explanation: High moisture causes rapid spoilage; drying, roasting, milling and hygienic packaging extend shelf life for months.

activities.definition: A device that automatically senses and regulates temperature inside a machine or oven
distractors: A wooden basket used to carry cassava from the farm
A receipt given by a supermarket cashier

activities.question: Why did Mensah refuse to print a fake registration number before passing the official FDA Ghana inspections?
options: Food safety, law and consumer trust come first; fake labels are illegal
He forgot how to use a printer
Supermarkets only buy food that has no label at all
activities.explanation: FDA Ghana registration protects public health and consumer trust; ethical businesses never fake safety approvals.

activities.question: When 100 packs cost 350 cedis (200 + 150) and sell for 500 cedis (100 × 5), what is the gross profit?
options: 150 cedis gross profit (30% of the 500-cedi revenue)
activities.explanation: Revenue (100 × 5 = 500 cedis) − Total Cost (200 + 150 = 350 cedis) = 150 cedis gross profit (150 ÷ 500 = 30%).

activities.prompt: Order the milestones that built Mansa and Mensah’s agro-processing company.
items: Study food science and accounting after spotting farm post-harvest losses.
Fix the uneven dryer and pass all FDA Ghana and GSA safety checks.
Grow over four years to employ 18 factory staff and support 45 farmers.
